title: Anthropic's $150 Wall Street target comes with a $900B catch
summary: Wall Street sees enormous upside for the Claude maker.
content: Anthropic’s record-breaking stock market debut was supposed to change AI investing. Instead, the company has painfully shown shareholders how quickly Wall Street sentiment can change. Shares of Anthropic (ANT) fell 6.5% on Nov. 24, closing at $81.91, below the $83 initial public offering price set less than a week earlier, according to MarketWatch . Now, several of the largest companies on Wall Street see an opportunity. Oppenheimer analyst Param Singh initiated coverage of Anthropic with an Outperform rating and a $150 price target, according to Seeking Alpha . The prognosis suggests an upside of around 83% from the Nov. 24 closing price for a company whose shares have already dropped precipitously since their public debut. There is a big problem with the optimism, however. In its SEC prospectus, Anthropic disclosed $900.9 billion in future purchase and lease commitments, mostly for computing infrastructure. These commitments span several years, with many extending into 2030. Whether Anthropic’s remarkable development potential will produce enough income and cash flow to support its massive infrastructure investments is a major question for shareholders. Wall Street sees major upside for Anthropic stock Despite the company’s poor first trading week, many investment firms are upbeat about Anthropic’s long-term potential. Oppenheimer’s Singh believes Anthropic is well-positioned to capture growing enterprise demand for artificial intelligence, according to Seeking Alpha’s Nov. 24 report . The firm forecasts Anthropic’s revenue will climb from an estimated $57.5 billion in 2026 to $275.1 billion in 2028, with operating margins exceeding 20%. Additionally, Oppenheimer projects that by 2030, the company’s whole addressable enterprise market may exceed $5.3 trillion. Singh pointed out that although typical expenditure accounts for less than 0.1% of those clients’ costs, more than half of Fortune 500 businesses now bring in at least $100,000 in trailing 12-month revenue for Anthropic. This indicates that when companies integrate Claude into more routine processes, Anthropic might significantly increase revenue from current clients. Oppenheimer is hardly the only company anticipating significant growth. According to CNBC and Seeking Alpha, three prominent firms have initiated bullish coverage of Anthropic: Oppenheimer: Param Singh initiated coverage with an Outperform rating and a $150 price target. Canaccord Genuity: David Hynes Jr. initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $135 price target. Wedbush: Ygal Arounian initiated coverage with an Outperform rating and a $120 price target. Even Wedbush’s more cautious $120 goal suggests an increase of around 47% from the Nov. 24 closing price. The optimism is a reflection of predictions that corporate AI investment will keep growing as businesses transition from testing to using AI technologies across their operations. But the estimates also show how Anthropic’s actual market success differs significantly from experts’ expectations. Anthropic’s $900 billion commitments create a major test One of the main issues confronting the recently public company is the vast computing resources needed for Anthropic’s rapid development. About $900.9 billion in total purchase commitments and leasing agreements, mostly pertaining to computer infrastructure, were revealed in its SEC prospectus. Of that amount, roughly $451.6 billion is expected to be incurred before Dec. 31, 2030, with the substantial remainder expected between 2031 and 2045, according to Anthropic . These obligations are not the same as debt that is due immediately. However, they represent substantial future expenditures that Anthropic will need to fund via its operations. Canaccord Genuity identified the company’s infrastructure commitments as a major financial risk when initiating coverage with a Buy rating and a $135 target, Investing.com reported. Canaccord projects that Anthropic’s earnings will be $55.2 billion in 2026, $136.4 billion in 2027, and $224.5 billion in 2028. Additionally, the company projects that by 2028, adjusted operating margins would be close to 20%. Analysts cautioned that if client demand rises more slowly than anticipated or computer equipment is underused, profitability may suffer. The difference is important because Anthropic is investing significant resources years before it has any idea of how much its consumers will eventually spend. Its ability to generate returns on those investments will be critical to determining whether Wall Street’s bullish forecasts prove justified. More Artificial Intelligence: AI investments fail when companies ignore the hard part of transformation Morgan Stanley issues a fresh warning about AI stocks CrowdStrike gives companies a ‘kill switch’ as bots go off script Anthropic gets a $150 Wall Street target with a massive catch. NurPhoto / Getty Images Why Anthropic analysts remain optimistic about Claude Analysts believe Anthropic will profit from a rising trend toward AI systems that carry out intricate commercial activities, despite the massive capital needs. Canaccord analysts believe the company’s potential market extends beyond traditional software spending into corporate labor and operating budgets. The company cited Claude Code as an example of customers delegating work to AI rather than simply using chatbots for information, Investing.com reported. Anthropic’s income potential might be greatly increased by such change. Oppenheimer also highlighted Anthropic’s ability to run Claude across several computing platforms, including Amazon (AMZN) Trainium, Google’s (GOOGL) tensor processing units, and graphics processors supplied by Nvidia (NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). This approach allows Anthropic to optimize workloads across different suppliers, potentially improving efficiency and reducing the cost of serving customers. Analysts did concede, however, that OpenAI, Google, and creators of open-weight AI models pose a serious threat to Anthropic. Even as demand for AI services increases, more competition may put pressure on costs. Oppenheimer also cautioned that the company’s large computing obligations, weaker user growth, and delayed business adoption could lead to liquidity and margin issues. Because Anthropic has to keep investing in more sophisticated models to stay competitive, the challenge is especially important. What Anthropic’s $150 target means for shareholders The contrast between investor trust in individual AI businesses and the enthusiasm around artificial intelligence is shown by Anthropic’s poor market debut. The stock opened at $111.50 during its Nov. 19 debut before reaching an intraday high of $115.10. Shares have dropped about 29% from that peak, with Nov. 24’s closing price at $81.91. However, Oppenheimer’s $150 target indicates that the company thinks Anthropic may become one of the largest winners of corporate AI usage. The discrepancy between the present market price and optimistic analyst projections highlights the significant uncertainty surrounding the company’s value. Investors will be watching Anthropic’s ability to sustain its rapid revenue growth, increase corporate adoption, and improve profitability while managing its infrastructure commitments. The development of more powerful AI models alone won’t be enough to secure the company’s survival; it will also be necessary to leverage that technology into long-term financial gains. Oppenheimer’s optimistic prediction takes advantage of this opportunity, and the risk is covered by Anthropic’s $900.9 billion in stated obligations. The final test for shareholders is whether the company can expand quickly enough to support both. Related: Anthropic’s $2 trillion debut hides a 13% warning

title: Elon Musk tells Tesla investors there is 'only one way' to eliminate poverty
summary: Musk says poverty won't end with government checks, and that Tesla is building the real answer.
content: Most CEOs pitch investors on margins and market share. Elon Musk is pitching them on ending poverty. The Tesla CEO has made Optimus, the company’s humanoid robot, the centerpiece of his case for Tesla’s future. In his view, it’s also the only realistic path to a world where nobody is poor. Read more: Elon Musk says treasury should just ‘issue people checks’ rather than taxing the rich Musk’s ‘only one way’ message to shareholders Musk didn’t frame Optimus as a cool gadget or a factory tool. He framed it as the fix for problems governments have chased for generations. “People often talk about eliminating poverty, giving everyone amazing medical care,” Musk said at Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting on Nov. 6, 2025. “Well, there’s actually only one way to do that, and that’s with the Optimus robot.” He didn’t leave much wiggle room. “Optimus will actually eliminate poverty,” he said. That was the same meeting where shareholders approved a pay package that could ultimately be worth up to $1 trillion, with targets that include putting 1 million Optimus robots to work. Musk boiled the pitch down further in a post on X on Nov. 16, 2025. “Optimus will eliminate poverty and provide universal high income for all,” he wrote. Also read: How much of Elon Musk’s net worth is in Tesla & SpaceX stock? Elon Musk says Telsa robots will make work optional. SOPA Images / Getty Images Universal high income, not basic income Universal basic income usually means a government check that covers the essentials. Musk is promising something bigger. “We’ll have, in a benign scenario, universal high income,” he said at the shareholder meeting. “Anyone can have any products or services that they want. But there will be a lot of trauma and disruption along the way.” He took it a step further on Dec. 17, 2025, when investor Ray Dalio said he would help seed Trump Accounts for children, following a $6.25 billion pledge from Michael and Susan Dell. “It is certainly a nice gesture of the Dells, but there will be no poverty in the future and so no need to save money. There will be universal high income,” Musk wrote in a reply on X. Read more: Elon Musk says Larry Page’s ‘Five Nines’ AI prediction is right, despite their decade-long feud Elon Musk once backed Buffett’s 5-minute fix for national debt: ‘This is the way’ Jeff Bezos predicts Amazon will eventually ‘go bankrupt’ and shares 30-year rule behind it What it means for Tesla investors For shareholders, the poverty pitch doubles as a valuation pitch. If Optimus can do what Musk says, the robot could matter far more to Tesla than its cars ever have. The robots are starting to roll. On Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 21, Musk said the company had “started what I’d call early production on our high-volume line in Fremont.” Tesla expects to begin delivering Optimus to outside companies around the end of 2027. Musk is still selling the demand side, too. “I think pretty much everyone’s going to want one, if not two,” he said at the TomorrowX Summit on Nov. 18. The catch Musk admits to Musk’s own words include a warning. The “trauma and disruption” he described is the stretch between today’s jobs and tomorrow’s abundance, and nobody knows how long it lasts. Worries about how AI will reshape the job market are already front and center. Musk’s plan also leaves unanswered questions about who owns the robots and how their output turns into income for regular households. Tesla investors have heard plenty of big promises over the years. Ending poverty may be the biggest yet, and Musk insists only one product can pull it off. Related: Mark Cuban delivers harsh truth about the one bill you’ll pay ‘for the rest of your life’

title: Goldman Sachs lays out three signals stock investors should watch
summary: Goldman Sachs reveals what it needs to see before stocks can find their footing. The market is not there yet.
content: Every selloff eventually runs out of sellers. The trick is spotting that moment before everyone else does, and investors are trying to do it after a slide that has erased roughly $8 trillion in market value since the Oct. 6 peak. Bargain hunters are circling, but nobody wants to catch the same falling knife twice. The panic was real. Wall Street’s fear gauge briefly spiked to 40 on Nov. 20. The kind of reading that tends to show up near a washout or right before something worse. Right now, the evidence points in both directions. Goldman’s three conditions offer a practical way to tell which one investors are facing this time. AI profits need to show up, not just promises Start with AI, since that is where this whole mess began. By Goldman’s estimate, the AI boom accounted for roughly half of the S&P 500’s earnings-per-share growth through September. So when doubts creep in about whether all that spending will pay off, it isn’t only Nvidia or Broadcom holders who feel it. Plain index fund investors feel it too. Also read: Morgan Stanley sends a strong signal on where stocks are headed The irony is that the latest numbers looked strong. Nvidia posted third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure. Interim CEO Colette Kress told investors it was “business as usual,” as reported by Inc. Revenue growth was never the problem. Even so, a blowout quarter was not enough to calm investors for long. The worry is less about today’s sales than tomorrow’s bills. Anthropic has committed about $900 billion to chips and AI infrastructure through 2045. Commitments on that scale are exactly what investors are now trying to price, and they want proof the revenue will arrive in time to cover them. Investors are asking the same question about every major AI spender. That helps explain why Anthropic’s record IPO couldn’t rescue the tape. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, well above its $83 offer price. It then tumbled on Nov. 20 because the debut failed to alleviate the spending concerns behind the broader AI selloff, according to Forbes. Investors clearly want earnings visibility, not just excitement. Don’t count on the Fed for a rescue Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider’s second catalyst, a dovish signal from the Federal Reserve, looks even further off. Markets still price in roughly 91% to 92% odds of a rate hike at the Fed’s Dec. 9 meeting, according to Yahoo Finance. That is hardly the backdrop that usually sparks a lasting rebound in growth stocks. Higher borrowing costs also make distant AI profits look less valuable today. Policymakers are not pushing back on those bets. Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned on Nov. 20 that delaying rate increases risks leaving the central bank behind the curve, Yahoo Finance reported. With consumer prices running about 4% above year-earlier levels, officials see little room to ease up. Big banks are adjusting to that reality. J.P. Morgan economists dropped their “one and done” view and now expect quarter-point hikes in December, January and March. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has argued that a half-point increase should be on the table in December. Until that hawkish chorus softens, a dovish surprise looks like the least likely of Snider’s three triggers. y Goldman’s estimate, the AI boom accounted for roughly half of the S&P 500’s earnings-per-share growth through September. Spencer Platt / Getty Images Positioning may already be washed out The third signal could be the closest to flashing. Morgan Stanley strategist Mike Wilson told clients the selloff delivered the capitulation and index catch-down he had been waiting for. He called the drop below his target range an overshoot of fair value, as reported by TheStreet. Wilson pointed to washed-out positioning and a volatility spike that reminded him of December 2018. He also noted the S&P 500 had fallen to about 16.4 times earnings, well below what he considers fair, and shifted to a much more bullish tactical view. More Goldman Sachs: Gas prices fall, but Goldman Sachs sees a $105 risk Goldman Sachs and Apollo changes position on SpaceX Goldman Sachs warns on the Hormuz crisis and rising fuel costs Traders on the ground saw the same exhaustion. Dan Niles covered his bets against stocks on Nov. 20, saying the market had reached “max pain.” When short sellers start heading for the exits, forced selling often fades quickly. That kind of short covering can fuel sharp rallies on its own. How strategists say to play it now Then came Nov. 23. Nvidia’s board put Jensen Huang back in the CEO chair, and the stock jumped more than 30% in a single session, Yahoo Finance reported. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 had their best day since April 2025, and Asian tech shares kept climbing on Nov. 24. If Snider’s first signal was ever going to show up, this is roughly what it would look like. Still, one big session is not a bottom, which is why Snider keeps recommending select defensives. Ron Insana also offers a similar playbook, urging investors heavy in tech to rebalance, raise some cash, and favor names like Berkshire Hathaway, Apple and Microsoft, as reported by TheStreet. His logic is simple: favor balance sheets that can fund themselves. The Anthropic debut is a useful warning for anyone tempted to chase the bounce. Buyers who paid the opening price were sitting on a nearly 13% loss by the first closing bell. Waiting for a second Goldman signal to confirm the first may be the smarter move. Related: Jim Cramer raises a red flag to stock market investors

title: Macy’s makes unprecedented Thanksgiving Day Parade decision
summary: The department store’s historic 100th parade celebration takes an unexpected turn.
content: For generations of Americans, Thanksgiving morning has meant turning on the television, watching giant balloons float through the streets of New York City, and catching a glimpse of Santa Claus before sitting down for the holiday feast. This year, that tradition will look a little different. Just hours before its landmark 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade, Macy’s announced on Nov. 25 that it would postpone the event because of severe weather expected to hit New York City. The parade will now take place on Saturday, Nov. 28, with an anticipated start time of 8:30 a.m. ET. It marks the first weather-related postponement in the parade’s history, dating back to 1924. The decision was made in consultation with New York City officials, with the safety of spectators, performers and volunteers in mind. In an official statement to NBC New York , a Macy’s spokesperson said, “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority.” Macy’s said it is working through the logistical challenges of rescheduling the event and will release additional details as they become available. Read more: Black Friday 2026: These retailers offer the biggest discounts Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed The department store had spent much of the year preparing for what was supposed to be one of its biggest holiday celebrations yet. As I wrote on Nov. 24 , the approaching nor’easter threatened to ground Macy’s signature giant balloons for the first time in 55 years. Now, the storm has forced organizers to reschedule the entire parade. New York City Emergency Management warned of wind gusts reaching 45 to 55 mph on Thanksgiving Day, along with 1 to 2 inches of rainfall and potential coastal flooding. The National Weather Service has since issued high-wind and coastal-flood warnings extending into Friday. More Retail: Struggling home goods chain closing more stores Verizon makes changes to be more like T-Mobile used to be Home Depot drops generous offers as customers grow harder to win Strong winds pose a particular challenge for Macy’s because of the parade’s signature giant character balloons. New York City safety regulations prohibit giant balloon flights when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts exceed 34 mph. While unfavorable weather has affected the parade in previous years, it has never forced organizers to move the entire event to another day. Even the Covid-19 pandemic did not stop Macy’s from holding the parade in 2020, although the retailer significantly scaled back the festivities and eliminated the traditional crowds along the parade route. The parade was canceled for three consecutive years, from 1942 to 1944, during World War II. The 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed. tarabird / Getty Images What Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponement means for viewers The last-minute decision also means a change in NBC’s programming and a potential disruption for tourists who traveled to New York specifically for the parade. NBC will broadcast a replay of the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at 8:30 a.m. across all time zones on Thanksgiving morning, the network confirmed in a statement to Entertainment Weekly . The rescheduled parade is expected to air on NBC and stream on Peacock on Saturday. Here is what viewers need to know: Original parade date: Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026 New parade date: Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026 Expected parade start time: 8:30 a.m. ET. Thanksgiving Day broadcast: A replay of the 2025 parade on NBC at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones Saturday broadcast: Expected to begin at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones on NBC and Peacock Visitors who planned to leave New York before Saturday may also have to reconsider their hotel and transportation arrangements if they still want to attend the historic celebration. The postponement could bring additional crowds to Manhattan during what is already one of the busiest shopping weekends of the year. Macy’s had big plans for its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade The postponement comes as Macy’s was hoping to build on the record-breaking success of last year’s event. The 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade attracted 35.7 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, an increase of 3.9 million viewers from the previous year, according to NBCUniversal’s 2025 year-end report . Viewership among audiences under 25 increased by 20%, according to preliminary Nielsen data released by NBCUniversal , highlighting the parade’s continued appeal to younger generations. For its 100th edition, Macy’s originally announced plans for: A record 100 inflatable parade elements More than 11,000 volunteers and participants New balloons featuring Bluey, Hello Kitty, and Disney’s Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey New floats from DoorDash, HBO, GEICO, and Planters Performances by Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Natasha Bedingfield, and other artists The event also serves as a major marketing opportunity for Macy’s and its brand partners at the start of the critical holiday shopping season. This year’s parade was designed to be the culmination of the retailer’s yearlong “Celebrations Start at Macy’s” marketing campaign. The commercial stakes are significant. Advertising spots during the 2023 parade averaged approximately $865,000 per 30 seconds, according to Guideline data cited by EMARKETER on Nov. 23. With the event now scheduled for the day after Black Friday, Macy’s will have to bring together thousands of performers, volunteers and commercial partners while the retailer navigates one of its most important sales weekends. Macy’s has not yet announced whether the postponement will result in changes to its originally scheduled entertainment lineup. Related: Walmart makes a major change at the cash register

title: Another healthy fast-food chain closes all its restaurants
summary: The shutdown follows True Food Kitchen's Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing and Salad and Go's abrupt shutdown.
content: People like the idea of healthy fast food more than they actually want to order it. It’s a battle between intention and reality. Everyone gets up in the morning, says they’re going to work out, and plans on eating a healthy lunch. When it actually comes time to do that, however, people skip chains like Sweetgreen, Salad and Go, and the just-shuttered Vinaigrette Salad Kitchen because they want to enjoy what they’re eating. We know what’s good for us, but don’t make healthy choices for a number of reasons. “Almost half of consumers — 46% — are aware they should eat healthier diets, but most of those — 71% — are not making changes, and the two biggest barriers to a healthier diet are cost and taste,” said Joseph Balagtas, professor of agricultural economics at Purdue, citing a 2025 survey conducted by his department. Nearly half of consumers cite the cost of healthier foods as a challenge, and 42% say they prefer the taste of their current diet, even if it’s not the healthiest. Restaurants don’t make money based on people’s best intentions. They need people to actually want to eat there, and salad-based chains simply don’t give people enough of what they want. Vinaigrette Salad Kitchen closing its final locations Vinaigrette Salad Kitchen had a simple slogan: “People Love a Salad Done Right.” The problem is that they don’t. They might say they do, but people actually like burgers, chicken nuggets, pizza, tacos, and pretty much anything else that isn’t good for them. Once a six-restaurant chain, Vinaigrette Salad Kitchen posted on its Facebook page that its final two locations would be closing after service on Nov. 25. “This isn’t goodbye to a restaurant; it’s goodbye to a community,” the company’s owners posted, and hundreds of people responded. More Restaurants: 40-year-old fast-food franchisee files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy Landry’s rescues 9 restaurants from bankruptcy as closures mount Outback Steakhouse restaurant franchisee files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy Michelle Rawlings’ post was typical of most of the messages. “I’m so sad, as the Harvest Kale Salad has been my favorite salad for years. Would you share the list of what’s in the dressing for that salad? I don’t know that I’m savvy enough to recreate it, but I’d like to try,” she wrote. Deborah Miller noted that this has become a trend. “First Core Life and now this!! Where are healthy food options?” she posted. True Food Kitchen remains under Chapter 11 bankruptcy but continues to operate. Shutterstock Healthy restaurants have struggled Gyms work because you have to pay your monthly membership fee whether you actually go there or not. Healthy restaurants need customers to actually show up and eat there. Vinaigrette Salad Kitchen isn’t isolated. It’s part of a trend that has hit a number of chains, including: Salad and Go Filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Aug. 5, 2026. Closed all 70 remaining restaurants. Previously closed 41 Texas restaurants in 2025 and another 32 locations in Texas and Oklahoma in January 2026. Had grown to approximately 146 locations before its retrenchment. Cited sustained pressure on consumer demand, past expansion problems, and rising costs. A July 2026 Cyclospora outbreak also hurt confidence in salads, although Salad and Go was not implicated. Its founders blamed declining food quality and price increases after selling the business. TheStreet : Healthy fast-food chain shuts down after Chapter 11 filing True Food Kitchen Filed Chapter 11 on Oct. 4, 2026. Closed 12 restaurants, leaving 34 locations operating across 14 states. Oprah Winfrey is an investor and board member. Secured approximately $20 million in debtor-in-possession financing. Plans to pursue a court-supervised sale. Reported sales of approximately $312 million in 2025, compared with $314 million the previous year. Reported debt was approximately $42 million, according to an attorney interviewed by TheStreet. TheStreet: Oprah-backed chain closes 12 restaurants after filing Chapter 11 Planta Filed Chapter 11 in May 2025. Reported between $10 million and $50 million in liabilities. Initially closed several restaurants, including West Palm Beach (CityPlace), Miami Beach, and other markets. A Delaware bankruptcy judge subsequently converted the case to Chapter 7 liquidation in March 2026. The chain’s upscale vegan concept faced a limited customer base and declining interest in plant-based food. Assets were previously sold for approximately $7.8 million during the Chapter 11 process. TheStreet: Vegan restaurant chain forced into Chapter 7 bankruptcy shutdown Veggie Grill Closed 12 restaurants, approximately 40% of its locations. The closures were part of a restructuring effort. The chain was acquired in January 2024 to avoid bankruptcy. Continues to face challenges in the plant-based restaurant category. TheStreet: Restaurant chain closed 40% of locations in Chapter 11 bankruptcy Slutty Vegan Founder Pinky Cole filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2026. The chain had shrunk from approximately 14 locations to just a handful. The company had expanded rapidly, becoming a nationally recognized vegan restaurant brand. Its financial problems illustrate the challenges of building a restaurant around a specialized food category. TheStreet: Popular vegan and vegetarian chains that closed or downsized LEON The British healthy fast-food chain exited the U.S. market in 2026. Closed all its U.S. restaurants. Subsequently entered administration in the U.K., a process broadly comparable to insolvency proceedings. Its menu focused on Mediterranean-inspired, natural fast food. TheStreet: 21-year-old fast-food chain is closing 20 restaurants amid comeback Neat Burger Vegan burger chain backed by Leonardo DiCaprio and Lewis Hamilton. Closed all its U.S. locations in May 2026. Had already closed its U.K. locations in 2025 and entered liquidation. Another example of the difficulty of scaling a restaurant concept around plant-based food. TheStreet: 22-year-old fast-food burger chain closes locations in bankruptcy And for good measure, Sweetgreen has seen its business shrink. “Same-store sales change was (6.4)%, reflecting a 4.9% decrease in traffic and a 2.1% decrease in product mix, partially offset by a 0.6% benefit from menu price increases implemented during the current year period,” the company shared in its third-quarter earnings report . Overall revenue did climb by 2.1% because the company opened 30 new locations over the past year, but the chain lost $30.1 million. TheStreet Americans don’t want healthy food “ How Major Restaurant Chains Plan Their Menus ,” an article that appeared in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, showed the challenges of offering healthy options and why many chains don’t. “Restaurants may try to avoid losing groups with a ‘health seeker’ by offering healthier foods (low in fat and calories, more fruits and vegetables) (27% of chains), but operators believe demand for healthier foods is not widespread. Additional obstacles to including healthier menu items are the short shelf life of produce (46%), increased preparation time, low sales, and high labor costs,” the data showed. Basically, a chain like Wendy’s may put a salad on the menu to appease a member of the group who might otherwise veto the chain. It’s doing that to sell more burgers and chicken nuggets, not because it thinks it’s going to turn Americans into salad eaters. The 2025 IFIC Food & Health Survey shows that Americans struggle with making healthy eating choices. The findings include: 79% say it’s hard to know what to believe because nutrition information keeps changing. 54% say eating healthy consistently is harder than doing their taxes. 58% say it’s harder than exercising regularly. 56% say it’s harder than getting eight hours of sleep. The annual study, which surveyed 3,000 people, also found that Americans think they’re getting less healthy. “In 2025, fewer than half of Americans (49%) describe their health as excellent (13%) or very good (35%), representing a notable 13-percentage-point decline from its peak. This sustained downward trend signals a meaningful shift in how Americans perceive their health,” the data showed. Salad restaurants sell a product that people say they want, but often pass up for something they enjoy more. That’s not going to change in any meaningful way, no matter how many chains open and close. Related: There’s one thing Trader Joe’s won’t do that customers want

title: Dollar Tree shoppers may soon pay more or get less
summary: Walmart, Kroger, and Publix might seem like they cost more, but there's a catch.
content: Dollar Tree stopped selling items for $1 back in 2024. Now, $1.25 serves as its entry-level price, but the company uses $2 as its baseline. “We strive to balance our $2 or below opening price points with our multi-price points and to balance our consumable and discretionary categories so that we offer multiple ways to meet all customers where they are across all economic cycles,” CEO Michael Creedon shared during the chain’s third-quarter earnings call . Mixed baskets, which combine multi-price and opening price point items, accounted for approximately 25% of Dollar Tree’s Q3 transactions, but nearly half of its sales. These baskets came in at more than 2.5 times the size of an opening price point basket. “That tells us something important. Customers continue to rely on our opening price points while adding multi-price items that deliver exceptional value and help them accomplish more in a single trip,” the CEO added. The chain’s pricing, however, has faced multiple challenges, and Creedon shared how Dollar Tree will address that. He was honest, and while he pledged a desire to hold prices steady, shoppers may not like some of the ways the chain is prepared to do that. Dollar Tree faces rising costs Creedon explained during the call how higher diesel prices have impacted Dollar Tree. “Domestically, we’re dealing with higher fuel costs and a tight driver market, and on imports, that pressure is coming from fuel. With respect to your sort of rule of thumb, the best way I could describe that is that on the 2/3, which is the domestic transportation, about $1 in diesel price is worth somewhere around $40 million of annual cost to us,” he said. On the import side, he made it clear that prices have gone up but that there’s no clear formula to share in that area. He also shared the five ways Dollar Tree can address higher costs, and consumers won’t like a couple of them: We’ve got supplier renegotiation to push back on the cost. Reengineering products and pack sizes to accommodate the price point. Discontinuing items that cannot meet the margin targets. We have seen a shift in countries of origin to accommodate the lowest-cost product. And finally, the last point for us is optimizing pricing. He was clear that raising prices was something the company saw as a “last step.” Dollar Tree’s opening price point is $1.25. Shutterstock Dollar stores might not be cheaper The Dollar Tree website , which shows in-store pricing, shows an awful lot of items at the $1.25 price point. What it doesn’t show is whether you’re getting less for your $1.25 than you did last time you visited. In addition, while the price might seem low, consumers may be paying more than they would at Walmart, Kroger, Publix, or any other regional grocery chain. “It’s a shame because, on the one hand, dollar stores can keep price points low. But the real shame here is that they serve communities that are already underserved, and sometimes the cost per unit is actually higher than what you would pay at another store,” RTM Nexus CEO Dominick Miserandino told TheStreet. For some shoppers, he noted, chains like Dollar Tree may be their only convenient option. “For communities that already have limited shopping options, this is another kick,” he wrote. More Retail: Struggling home goods chain closing more stores Verizon makes changes to be more like T-Mobile used to be Home Depot drops generous offers as customers grow harder to win Finance Buzz ‘s comparison of Walmart and Dollar Tree prices, updated in November, illustrates Miserandino’s point. “A single roll of 451-sheet Charmin Essentials Strong runs $1.25 at Dollar Tree. Buy 18 rolls one at a time, and you spend $22.50, compared to $15.67 for an 18-pack at Walmart. That is about $6.83 extra, or roughly 87 cents a roll versus $1.25,” the article showed. That was not an isolated incident. “The pattern repeats elsewhere. Dollar Tree sells 3.5-ounce packs of Cinnamon Toast Crunch for $1.25, about 36 cents an ounce, and six-tablet Advil bottles for the same price. Small packaging quietly raises the real cost per serving,” the site reported. Pricing, it should be noted, varies by store and date. Still, it’s generally true that at dollar stores, you’re paying more per serving, so to speak. Dollar Tree has rarely raised prices While telling consumers that he could raise prices or shrink how much you get when buying an item, Creedon also made it clear that the chain has only “taken price at scale twice” in its 40-year history. “The competition is changing their pricing all the time. When we have to take price, which we did last year in the inflationary cost environment that we were in, the worst day for us is the day we take price. Every day after that, we get better,” he said. Creedon also cited that the chain offers a shopping experience that many associate with Costco, TJ Maxx, and Marshalls. “And so we like the position we’re in, zeroed in on that value, convenience, and still providing kind of guilt-free thrill-of-the-hunt pleasure and discovery,” he added. title: Whole Foods is open on Thanksgiving, but there’s an early deadline
summary: The grocery chain is keeping many stores open for Thanksgiving as several major competitors close for the holiday.
content: Even the most organized Thanksgiving hosts can find themselves scrambling for a forgotten ingredient on the morning of the holiday. But finding a grocery store that’s open on Thanksgiving has become more challenging as many of the nation’s largest retailers are keeping their doors closed on Turkey Day. Walmart , Target , Costco , and Sam’s Club are among the major retailers that will be closed on Thursday, Nov. 26, as TheStreet previously reported. Grocery chains Publix , Aldi, and Trader Joe’s will also be closed on Thanksgiving, according to the companies. Also Read: Kohl’s confirms store closures during a critical shopping week BJ’s Wholesale Club confirmed to TheStreet that its locations will be closed for the holiday, too. While Thanksgiving was once considered the unofficial start of Black Friday shopping, many retailers now give employees the holiday off while offering Black Friday deals online and starting their sales earlier in November. For grocery shoppers, however, waiting until Black Friday to make a purchase isn’t always an option. Whether it’s an extra stick of butter, a carton of heavy cream, or a dessert for unexpected guests, some purchases simply can’t wait until the following day. And not all grocery retailers are taking the same approach to the holiday. Amazon-owned Whole Foods Market is giving shoppers an opportunity to make last-minute grocery runs on Thanksgiving, although customers shouldn’t wait until too close to dinnertime to head to their neighborhood store. More Retail: Restaurants open on Thanksgiving include McDonald’s and Dunkin’ Kroger is open on Thanksgiving, but there’s a catch Best Buy sticks with major nationwide store closure plans Whole Foods Thanksgiving hours 2026: When do stores close? Many Whole Foods stores will be open with adjusted hours on Thanksgiving, according to the company’s official holiday hours page . Most locations are expected to open, but hours may be shortened, Parade reports . The Associated Press also reports early closures. Shoppers can check their local store’s Thanksgiving hours using the Whole Foods store locator . CVS, Walgreens, Whole Foods, Starbucks, and McDonald’s are among the chains with locations open on Thanksgiving, Nov. 26, 2026. Hours and participation vary by location. Graphic: Kelly Tyko/TheStreet Whole Foods has a different policy for Christmas While Whole Foods gives customers an opportunity to shop on Thanksgiving, the grocery chain has a different policy for Christmas Day. Whole Foods stores will be closed Dec. 25. Many locations will also operate with modified hours on Christmas Eve, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day. title: IRS has a 21-day rule that could protect savings
summary: Most people miss this brief window before their money disappears.
content: You open your banking app one morning to check a balance, and the number sitting there reads a flat zero against every expectation. A short message from your bank reveals that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has placed a legal hold on the account. That scenario plays out across the country each year for Americans having unpaid federal tax balances somewhere in their financial history. Most account holders learn about the agency’s seizure powers only after the damage has already appeared on their banking screen. The panic that follows usually centers on one belief: that the money is gone and cannot be recovered quickly. That assumption overlooks a protection written into federal law , which gives taxpayers a narrow window before the funds leave the account. What usually triggers an IRS bank levy An IRS bank levy rarely happens without prior warning, although it may surprise taxpayers who have overlooked or ignored collection notices sent by the agency. Before seizing funds from a bank account, the IRS must generally issue a Notice and Demand for Payment, followed by a Final Notice of Intent to Levy at least 30 days before the levy takes effect. The final notice also informs taxpayers of their right to request a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing under Internal Revenue Code Section 6330 . Taxpayers generally have 30 days from the notice date to request a hearing using Form 12153 . Also read: IRS bills retired couple abroad over $7,000 a year If the taxpayer fails to respond, resolve the outstanding debt, or exercise applicable appeal rights, the IRS may proceed with the levy by sending Form 668-A to the financial institution. This directs the bank to freeze funds in the account, up to the amount of the outstanding tax liability. According to IRS Publication 594 , the agency generally resorts to levies after assessing the tax, issuing a bill, establishing that the taxpayer has neglected or refused to pay, and providing the required final notice at least 30 days before the seizure. As a result, IRS bank levies commonly affect taxpayers who have failed to address outstanding tax debts or respond to collection notices over an extended period. How the 21-day holding period works A bank that receives a levy must hold the funds for weeks before remitting any portion of the balance to the IRS. The institution must wait 21 calendar days after the levy is served before sending any payment, under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 6332(c) . Only funds present on the day the levy is imposed are frozen, meaning payroll or benefit deposits made thereafter remain accessible, according to the IRS’s bank levy guidance . A bank levy also captures only a snapshot of the account, so the IRS often issues additional levies if the first falls short. More Personal Finance: Fidelity shows health care costs outpacing inflation Jean Chatzky sees a retirement problem $1 million may not fix Dave Ramsey limits family lending to one of two options The 21-day period exists so the depositor can settle ownership disputes or hardship issues before any money reaches the Treasury, the IRS confirmed . The countdown begins the day the bank receives the levy notice, which often falls before the account holder spots the hold, the IRS noted . Missing that distinction costs most taxpayers crucial days of their window, since many discover the hold only after bills start bouncing or payroll fails. The IRS gives taxpayers 21 days to dispute a bank levy before frozen funds are transferred, making prompt action essential. Pekic / Getty Images How to request a release before day 22 Reaching the IRS collection line directly begins the release process within the holding period, since the bank has no authority to lift the hold. Grounds for release include proof that the debt was already paid, the collection window expired, or the taxpayer entered an installment agreement. Procedural errors and wrongful-levy claims qualify when the taxpayer proves the seizure hit the wrong account or bypassed notices. Economic hardship offers another path when the levy blocks payment of reasonable living expenses measured against the IRS Collection Financial Standards. John Zandi, Director and Founder of Detaxify, has urged taxpayers to move quickly once the bank sends its notification, USA Today reported . The 21-day holding period is often the taxpayer's best opportunity to recover some or all of the funds, Under IRC § 6532(c) , missing the window forces a harder path, since recovery after day 22 requires a wrongful-levy claim filed within two years of the levy. Taxpayers unable to reach the main IRS line can turn to the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) , an independent organization inside the IRS. The TAS, which can request a levy release when a taxpayer faces economic hardship, may be reached before the 21-day window closes. Steps to take the moment a levy notice arrives A levy notice does not mean the money is already gone, giving taxpayers an opportunity to act before the collection process advances. Those facing financial hardship can submit Form 911 to request faster assistance from the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) when regular IRS channels cannot respond quickly enough. Gathering documents that show essential living expenses is another important step. Pay stubs, rent receipts, utility statements, and medical bills help the IRS determine whether the seizure leaves enough money for basic needs, according to its Collection Financial Standards . Taxpayers should also contact the IRS immediately using the number provided on the levy notice, TAS advises . If the agency approves a release, written confirmation through Form 668-D ensures the bank receives formal instructions before the 21-day holding period expires, the IRS explains . An installment agreement may offer another resolution, but releasing a levy does not erase the underlying tax debt or prevent future collection action, the IRS cautions .
